title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
AI-generated images and videos were used to impersonate a real, named immigration attorney across multiple social media platforms. The fabricated content directed users to a WhatsApp number, where fraudsters presented fake contracts and collected payments through digital payment apps. This is an impersonation scheme, one in which generative AI tools lowered the cost and effort of producing convincing fake personas at scale.

The failure did not occur inside a single AI product with a discoverable design flaw. Instead, freely available or accessible generation tools were applied externally to create fraudulent content, which the platforms then hosted. The volume of removals, nearly 6,500 profiles across TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram, shows that platform-level detection did not stop the spread before significant harm occurred. Catching this earlier would have required either automated detection of synthetic media impersonating real individuals or faster human review of flagged accounts.

What is not established is who the scammers are, whether any investigation has produced findings, or how many victims beyond the cases reported actually lost money.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, reports that scammers are using artificial intelligence to create fake videos and social media profiles impersonating him. The criminals use AI-generated images and videos to offer immigration services Leal never provides, targeting vulnerable immigrants seeking legal help. Scammers request payments of thousands of dollars, including a $2,200 fee for fake US residency assistance. Leal first discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, though suspicious activity began last October and has escalated dramatically over the past three months.

His firm hired an anti-piracy company that has removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The scams typically start with social media videos directing viewers to contact a WhatsApp number, where fraudsters send fake contracts and request payment through digital apps like Venmo and Zelle. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate. He advises immigrants seeking legal services online to verify identities and avoid anyone requesting immediate payment through social media.
